This study proposes a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets without sacrificing the ability to forecast and interpret results. Furthermore, we have found that such models can effectively identify various underlying sources of volatility and volatility patterns in multiple contexts by analyzing the time series of rates derived from the raw count data. To validate the performance and versatility of our proposed model, we applied it to several case studies involving diverse data sets, including global trade sanctions, animal migration patterns, and website traffic fluctuations, among others.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a byproduct. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. We also utilized a sophisticated forward modeling approach that considers the full image formation process, including the effects of atmospheric scattering, telescope optics, and detector behavior, to obtain precise calibration from the data collected.

Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the chain rule of calculus and a second-order numerical integration of Brownian motion, a new method called Nornwd is proposed, offering enhanced precision in short-time configurational calculations. Results demonstrate that higher accuracy in numerical methods reduces the precision of subsequent approximations like the Born-Oppenheimer hypothesis, necessitating longer-time step sizes that can lead to significant errors in impulse resolution. Ultimately, enhanced precision in short-time calculations yields more extensive integrations of molecular dynamics, resulting in better-bo-renhnppy accuracy and highly precise Born-von Karmnnn configurations for resolving biomolecular impulses with substantial stiffness. Ultimately, results show that enhanced precision in short-time numerical integrations leads to highly precise born-von-karman configurations resolving biomolecular impulses and yielding slightly less precise bo-renppy configurations.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines tailored for image description, akin to what exists for image classification and description. These guidelines would help assess which scenarios are suitable for system evaluation and those that are not.

Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key unifying framework, based on the hydrodynamic expansion applicable to highly excited states and operators, has been developed and explored in this research. A theoretical, hydrodynamic-based formula for state and operator complexity in higher excitations is proposed and examined in the context of both constant time and conjugate time optimizations. A novel hydrodynamic leading order equation of state is derived and justified through microscopic field theoretic considerations. A comparison with existing exact solutions is also presented to validate the universality of the equation of state. A generalized hydrodynamic approach is suggested for tackling states and operators with even greater levels of excitation. A comprehensive summary of the hydrodynamic framework is also provided in the concluding section of the research.

The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while keeping energy scale assumptions low. In this bilepton model's framework, several decay pathways are examined, along with the resulting bilepton mass limits derived from data. Notable discrepancies are highlighted between the bilepton model's predictions and those of other models involving only a single extra heavy neutral particle. The bilepton model calls for complex decay patterns, including multiple generations of particle cascades and diverse end products such as baryons, antibaryons, mesons, and exotic particles like xions and bileptons, which can spontaneously disintinate into mesons. To validate this model, high energy thresholds of at least $10^4$ times that of the weak force are required, along with specific end product stability requirements. However, current experiments have not observed these predicted ends products, leading to ongoing research into ends product stability alternatives and further experiments. Alternative ends product stability options include leakage mechanisms, hidden sectors, and other unexplored options like unstable xions and bileptons. Unstable bileptons can cascade into mesons which can then form unstable clusters that can escape detectors without being observed. Alternative options include dark radiation and leakage mechanisms, as well as confined bileptons that can form dark nuclei within hidden sectors. In addition

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveform that required bespoke hardware.
An optimal narrowband waveform is used as a training signal to enable the training-free, massively multiplexed user screening process.
Mathematical results show that the user screening time grows linearly with the number of active users, but remains constant with bandwidth expansion, benefiting from using SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM signals.

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward task, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex challenge. Each relevant prediction, such as those for PDF behavior, may require specific transformations and adjustments before integration. Here, we outline the key steps needed to integrate and normalize theoretical predictions, highlighting the need for a common framework and standardized tools. Given the varying nature of inputs like kinematic ranges, error estimates, and systematic uncertainties, as well as the diverse transformation requirements, developing such a framework is essential. This paper serves as a call to action for a collaborative effort to establish this framework and the accompanying toolset, ultimately streamlining the process of PDF fitting.

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is demonstrated using an eddy-break-up model and a progress variable model. Results show that using an active flame approach yields more accurate outcomes by producing resonance frequencies that match observed values and preventing excessive growth rates that don't align with experimental data.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. The nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to show that de Sitter spacetime does not meet the theory's requirements.

This paper discusses recent findings from the LHC concerning small systems studied by the ALICE, ATLAS, and CMS collaborations. Due to the growing interest in quantum chromodynamics within small systems, particularly in brief note presentations, this session allocates an extended time for these discussions.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free drawing and thus enhancing visualization clarity.

In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique, HyperDegrade, which incorporates previous methods and employs simultaneous multithreading architectures.  A unique three-part model has been developed to predict the behavior of applications in order to maximize performance degradation, which was validated through various side-channel acceleration experiments, including Raccoon and a modified version of ShareMIA.  Compared to existing techniques, HyperDegrade demonstrates more significant improvements, particularly in the ShareMIA variant where it achieves a significant reduction in resolution requirements.

A localized alteration in knot diagrams is referred to as an unknotting operation. It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be transformed into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory; they serve a purpose in analyzing the intricacy of knots and knot-related properties. Moreover, they also have implications in the fields of biology, chemistry, and physics for studying complexly intertwined structures of molecules, substances, and DNA. The purpose of this paper was to introduce a novel type of unknotting operation, which is called the diagonal move, applicable to classical and welded knots. The study shows that the cross-over change, the delta-move, the sharp-move, the gamma-move, the n-gamma-move, the cluster-move, the 7-gamma-move, the 8-gamma-move, the 9-gamma-move, and the nu-move can be achieved through a series of diagonal moves. The study also delves into the computation of the minimum number of cross-overs that can be achieved through a sequence of diagonal moves, which is referred to as the diagonal distance, and examines its relationship to other distance measures. The research presents proof that the diagonal distance is equivalent to the minimum number of times a diagram can be transformed into itself by cutting and reattaching segments, which is called the ni-cluster

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, tasks need to be executed in complex environments that are highly dynamic and uncertain. An example of such a system is a group of robotic vehicles working together to find and rescue people after a disaster. To address these challenges, we propose a new approach that uses game theory to determine the best course of action for each agent. This approach aims to reach a state of equilibrium where no agent can benefit from changing their behavior unilaterally, using an implicit communication system that relies on the environment to share information. Through numerical examples, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this new method in various scenarios, including situations where information about the environment is uncertain and scenarios that are too complex to fully specify.

In our study, we developed a resolution for the wreath products of two groups that have resolution one, excluding the case where both groups are the infinite cyclic group. This research builds on the findings of Laszlo Szabo and contributes to the ongoing knowledge in group theory.

The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in areas with many users. As a result of the substantial size of MIMO arrays and the quantum small wavelength of high-frequency signals like millimeter wave, MIMO array responses are considered nearly orthogonal in high-dimensional signal spaces, enabling efficient signal space division multiplexing. Under these circumstances, random signal space encoding and decoding algorithms are considered effective and scalable, and low-overlap MIMO array patterns can be efficiently packed using area filling optimization techniques like FitPack, leading to an optimal or near-optimal utilization of available MIMO array patterns. Under laboratory conditions resembling real-world scenarios with many users in high-dimensional signal spaces, low-overlap MIMO array pattern packing efficiency of over 90% has been achieved through area optimization.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on task generation and model editing, we found that this approach is easily adjustable, allows for compositional manipulation of language knowledge, and achieves comparable performance to fully trained neural models while maintaining the compositional properties of $n$-gram models.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation rates and temperature differences between the equator and the poles. To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms, including the Coriolis and thermal driving forces. When the experiment uses very slow planetary rotation rates or a significant equator-to-pole temperature difference, multiple strong air currents, known as jets, form in the atmosphere. To further analyze the results, a graph is presented that maps different combinations of experimental conditions leading to single or multiple jet formations. To better understand the conditions under which multiple jets form, a theoretical model is proposed that predicts the number of possible multiple-jet states based on experimental conditions. To validate this model, various experiments are conducted that verify its accuracy.

This study formulates a genuine integral expression of the reciprocal gamma function in terms of a modified hypersingular integral. It also proves the connection to the traditional complex representation, in addition to obtaining a modified complex representation following the standard Hankel path.

Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, despite their limited accuracy, with a notable exception of a Bose-Einstein condensate's dynamics under intense laser pulses, which required a more advanced model. This paper extends this advanced phase-space description for interacting Bose gas systems, deriving a stochastic quantum-field equation that can simulate these dynamics, building on a positive phase-space formalism. This new stochastic Gross-Pitaevskii equation (SGPE) model fills a critical gap in previous models by incorporating a system's quantum fluctuations and mean-field dynamics, guided by an example of Bose gas systems transitioning between different spinor components under external forces. We also propose an efficient importance sampling algorithm to accelerate this simulation process and successfully demonstrate it through Bose gas systems precessing under magnetic fields, revealing the emergence of quantum vortex rings as a byproduct.

Deep Neural Networks with vast parameters have faced challenges in real-time deployment, prompting the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in knowledge distillation. These architectures feature a complex "Teacher" network guiding a streamlined "Student" Network. Knowledge distillation has been applied in various contexts including scene comprehension, semantic image editing, and object recognition. The field of scene comprehension presents a Knowledge Distillation Framework called Cross蒸馏 that integrates background knowledge from both words and images to assist a simplified Student Criss-Cross Attention Architecture. In addition, knowledge distillation plays a crucial role in low-resolution imagery analysis and serves as a predictive tool for scene grammar. Our Teacher-Student Architecture contributes to knowledge distillation, low-resolution scene understanding, and image-to-image mapping alongside high-resolution scene analysis. Experimental results on scene graphs, image segmentation, and rendering demonstrate the effectiveness of the Teacher-Student Architecture. Our Research Distilled Scene Representation achieves state-of-the-art outcomes on Scene Graph Generation, Scene Acknowledgement, and Scene Understanding and Imaging tasks.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX and Gurobi for constrained optimisation, when evaluated on a wide range of synthetic and real-world graphs. Our FABE approach achieves this by a factor of at least 100 times in terms of induced variable size, while still maintaining the accuracy of results, specifically with a 5% reduction in memory usage and a 300% improvement in computational time for the best-performing real-world data set.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$, which, as per our research, has centralizer $E(n)$ in $C{\left({\left(U{\left(sl2)^{n}}\right)}\right)}$ for its natural diagonal embedding, found within its own structure. Through its quotient by its ideal of zero divisors, we construct a relevant algebra then, as per our research findings, prove its isomorphism to the centralizer $E(n)$. We then embed the modified Racah algebra within the $n$-tensor centralizer repeatedly to obtain the $n$-tensor centralizer as a final result. To do this for the general su(m) case, we extend our approach accordingly, with the centralizer of the $n$-tensor $U(su(m))$ centralizer found the same way. As per our main theorem, we find the centralizer's isomorphism within the $n$-tensor centralizer of the general $U(su(m))$ special algebra, then obtained the same way, consequently.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces systems to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an exact paired-permutation test algorithm that can efficiently process high-dimensional data sets. Our Java implementation shows that the exact method can significantly reduce computation time compared to existing Monte Carlo approaches, achieving exact results that match Monte Carlo approximations within a 0.0005 confidence interval. In addition, our analysis of data distribution reveals that paired-permutation tests don't conform to a normal distribution, justifying the need for exact algorithms. Furthermore, we've created an optimized variant of the exact algorithm that can achieve more precise results in a shorter amount of time.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles.

This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are organized on a grid. A streamlined variation of the Rao-Blackwellized point mass filter predicts the density of unobserved targets, with their distribution approximated as Gaussian for initially detected targets. Contrary to conventional implementations, the method presented utilizes grid-based variations to represent unobserved target densities. As a result, sharp boundaries can be created around areas within the region of interest that fall outside of a sensor's field of view, all without employing an excessive number of Gaussian mixture components, which reduces the computation required. A sensor management scenario is also explored where control over the movement of sensors is optimized in a region of interest, with limited fields of view, in search of targets.

The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely focused on analyzing them. Video footage of these situations is readily available, yet decisions on the best course of action remain the coach's responsibility. During these moments, with limited time, vast amounts of information can be overwhelming, making it hard to determine what's most important and what action to take. An automated system that provides concise recommendations could potentially aid coaches in making better decisions. In this study, the complexity of situations is broken down into key components, and a policy is optimized using reinforcement learning by analyzing the footage of these situations. To test the system's effectiveness, it was applied to games played in the Dutch Eredivisie league, where it analyzed situations that were deemed critical, such as goals scored, teams scored, and games ended. The resulting images showcasing the situation's features and the team's current score were used to evaluate the system's performance. Results showed that in situations where the system's chosen action led to a goal, it outperformed the actions taken by players 61% of the time during games where the system was used. Additionally, the system's actions aligned with the game's outcome 57% of the time, demonstrating its potential to provide valuable insights into situation dynamics. However, more research is needed to determine if recognized situations can predict the game's outcome effectively.

We provide explicit definitions for solitary wave solutions that emerge in a Klein-Gordon equation and prove their stability against spectral disturbances. These solutions, constructed for a mass-constrained system, reflect the complex dynamics observed in physical phenomena like solar wind plasma. Our findings, which fill gaps in research by providing explicit examples and proving stability, offer new insights into the spectral stability of solitary wave solutions in a nonlinear field equation.

In experiments involving particle collisions, identifying neutral long-lived particles relies on either finding decay products at unusual locations or missing energy. The choice between these methods depends on the particle's properties, such as how far it travels before decaying and whether it leaves a trace. To improve our ability to discover new particles, the Belle II experiment is conducting a detailed study of the $B^+ \to K^+ axion(\rho^0)$ decay process. By analyzing data from this experiment, we can estimate how likely Belle II is to find certain types of low-proportionality-like particles produced from $B$ bar collisions, specifically those lasting more than a tenth of a second and those that leave a trace but last less than a second. This involves considering various types of particles, including those that decay into electron positron pairs and those that remain stable, such as dark matter and millicharged particles. For specific particles like dark scalars and dark axion-like particles, we evaluate the effectiveness of different detection methods, including direct detection and looking for their production in conjunction with other particles. We also examine the possibility of detecting these particles by analyzing their decay processes, such as the $D^0$ to $K^0$ S transition. Based on this analysis, we can determine the minimum probability that Belle II can find these particles, depending on their proportion in collisions and their characteristics like speed and charge. This study meticulously examines the performance of state-of-the-art semantic change detection models, specifically contextualized language models like ERE and SES, which have been evaluated using the WordSenseIndicators dataset spanning a 200-year period. Our analysis involves a substantial reorganization and enrichment of the WSI dataset, dividing it into multiple sub-datasets based on context segments. By assigning contextualized embeddings to these sub-diagnostics and graphing their distribution, we are able to identify instances of semantic shift, independent of metadata. Our findings indicate that contextualized embeddings are effective in detecting synchronic semantic changes but may be hindered in detecting diachronic changes. We propose a revised dataset organization strategy that could help mitigate this issue.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) contain black holes with massive spins that can potentially evolve into intermediate-mass black holes. Due to their high masses, their electromagnetic spectra show significant modifications, particularly near the photon sphere where spin-related effects are most pronounced. These effects can help researchers understand the characteristics of black holes, including their mass and spin, as well as the properties of the surrounding accretion disk. In this study, we investigate the effects of active galactic nuclei black holes with various masses, ranging from $10^3$ to $10^9$ solar masses, with spins of 0.9 and 0.99. We analyze different agency models, including the minimization of total disk radiation, the assumption of constant gas supply, and the consideration of gas supply driven by buoyancy. Our research involves generating theoretical curves that can be used to train machine learning algorithms, specifically neural networks, to analyze electromagnetic spectra, particularly thermal disk spectra. We develop a four-layer neural network model that can accurately determine the mass and spin of active galactic nuclei containing black holes. Our results demonstrate that by analyzing modified thermal disk spectra, particularly those affected by strong relativistic effects, researchers can effectively determine the mass and spin of active galactic nuclei with various gas supply models. We also explore the impact of adding noise to the spectra on the accuracy of mass and spin measurements. Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to quantify and express Antecedent and Consequent expectations as introduced in (Wang et al., 2020), allowing to reason about a program's performance metrics such as runtime and resource usage. To enable this expansion, we expect the quantum computer's control software to provide precise documentation on reasoning about post-circuit transformations, enabling quantification over relationships between programs' outcomes. As a bonus, we also present relational correctness proofs for linear operators acting on adjacent programs and diagonal measurement-based programs that yield quantum classical hybrid programs' outcomes.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias and distinguish it from standard magnetic field concentration measures. Subsequently, various inversion algorithms are tested using synthetic data with known parameters, allowing for the tracing of bias sources. Finally, the study applies these insights to real data, examining vector magnetic field maps obtained from a high-resolution spectrometer, the IMaX instrument on the Swedish 1m telescope. At this resolution, a significant Bperp bias is found but can be effectively mitigated by employing a higher resolution dataset as a constraint during the inversion process. The findings are deemed to be directly applicable to similar low-resolution vector magnetic field scans, facilitating more accurate vector magnetic field maps, especially in stellar atmospheres where high-resolution spectra may be scarce.

For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a crucial decision, yet there has been limited investigation into its implications, particularly within the context of deep learning. We contend that an analytical framework for assessing the performance of various loss functions is urgently needed. We performed an extensive experiment, utilizing a fixed architecture for a neural network, and tested it with 10 commonly used loss functions, across 100 classification tasks on two large-scale datasets: CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. Our main findings revealed that on the ImageNet dataset, nearly all loss functions yielded comparable results, with cross entropy and its variants leading the pack. We observed that the choice of loss function had a more pronounced effect on the CIFAR-10 dataset. Our results also indicated that all loss functions could effectively train a neural network, albeit with varying training speeds and final training losses. We found that the decision to employ supervised classification and the objective to minimize training loss are largely compatible, regardless of the specific loss function chosen. We believe our findings pave the way for future research, focusing on developing an analytical framework for loss functions, particularly by exploring regulated training, assigning training targets, and assigning training losses.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 25.3%, 13.6%, and 51.1% respectively, all within a short training period of 2 epochs.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet), demonstrates superior accuracy in detecting conditions like ventricular septal defects compared to existing research.  The findings provide a foundation for creating low-cost heart monitoring devices that can be used in resource-limited areas.

We analyzed a sample of 101 galaxies for which data is available for two specific fine structure lines of neutral atomic carbon, and we found their average conditions to be significantly non-equilibrium. Based on exact solutions of a 3-level system without any assumptions regarding hydrogen gas properties, we found the line formation process to be responsible for observed variations in atomic and molecular gas temperatures. We also found standard metrics to be non-applicable for atomic molecular gas thermal equilibrium and equilibrium lines radiative excitation conditions, and we proposed atomic non-LTE excitation temperature and equilibrium line excitation temperature as alternatives. We found significant agreement between these alternative temperatures and dust temperatures, and we concluded for any given galaxy that atomic non-LTE excitation temperature, dust temperature, and molecular gas temperature are in equilibrium, whereas for traditional three-color dust equilibrium to be in effect only atomic non-LTE excitation temperature and dust temperature are in equilibrium.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time approaches infinity. This conclusive finding addresses two contrasting limits observed for first-class particles in vacuum and discrete steps, as well as the lack of equilibrium in ASEP.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic, with a focus on differential integral models introduced by Kermack and McKendrick. We examine fundamental characteristics of these models, demonstrate their connection to probability theory, and explore their limitations. Due to its relevance to probability theory and stochastic analysis, we discuss potential extensions of these models. As a result of our findings, a mathematical framework is proposed for establishing a stochastic process that models epidemic spreading.

Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 2200 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are likely to have a lower specific star formation rate within the bulge and a higher bulge-to-disc ratio, as evidenced by the $uv-r$ color and BTD050300 index. Furthermore, galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater are more probable to have a short bulge timescale of less than a billion years. In contrast, an image showing the correlation between star formation rates and stellar mass constructed using only the outer parts of galaxies would suggest that bulge

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize Croatian news articles as
expressing positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, employing a dataset from
Slovene. The underlying model is a multilingual BERT-based system, fine-tuned
on the available data. To bridge the linguistic gap, the study utilizes
pre-trained sentiment models for Slovene. The assessment involves testing
various combinations of models and embeddings, along with exploring different
processing methods for supervised, few-shot, and zero-shot learning scenarios.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we anticipate a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9067861's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies to resolve this intriguing puzzle.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive and time-consuming. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system has been proposed on emerging events by leveraging multi-modal content found on social media platforms. This system consists of concept generation, feature extraction, and clustering sections, allowing for the identification of unknown false news as well as its image manipulation detection and cross-modal embedding without the need to label the newly emerging events. Experiments conducted on three datasets demonstrate the system's effectiveness in detecting false news as well as the unknown concept and its cross-modal retrieval capabilities.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, GCA pairs are constructed in 10 and 12 dimensions, and quadruples in 10^2, 12^2, 10*12, and 2*10^2 - 4 dimensions. Additionally, the research extends GCA quadruples to higher dimensions, resulting GCAQ quadruples in 10^4, 12^4, 10^2*12^2, 2*10^4 - 2^2 dimensions, as well 10^3*12^3, 2*10^3*12^3, 10^4*12^4, 2*10^4*12^4 dimensions. A set of GCA quadruples are also constructed in 32^4, 64^4, 128^4 and 256^4 dimensions.

A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response to this challenge, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by incorporating a diverse range of training data features. Experimental results show that this framework significantly improves segmentation accuracy when compared to common image processing techniques, with a 6.74% improvement in Dice Score and a 50% reduction in error rate, demonstrating the framework's effectiveness in evaluating the outcomes of LITT therapy. This research contributes to the development of new and effective treatments for brain lesions while advancing the field of medical image processing and deep learning.

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained significant interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing features that maximize information gain. The subsequent step employs contrastive learning to optimize features, with similar data points projecting to adjacent areas on the feature manifold and dissimilar ones to opposite regions. The final step outputs the feature set through all-encompassing optimization. Our framework's innovative all-positive contrastive learning method enables similar data points to expand their dimensional space while compressing the space for dissimilar points. Our framework's theoretical analysis proves its ability to output feature sets that meet similarity-based optimization goals. Our framework's experimental results on real-world datasets, including text, image, and video data, demonstrate its superior performance compared to existing methods.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained on knowledge infused with knowledge graphs exhibit superior performance compared to those trained on textual representations of knowledge. Specifically, our approach shows that K-GPT, a 139-parameter model, outperforms traditional methods in downstream tasks such as semi-supervised natural language inference and named entity recognition. Furthermore, we anticipate that structured knowledge graphs can be more efficiently optimized compared to vast corpora of text.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), finding that the transition temperature decreases as the YM charge parameter increases.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of a given light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects manifesting in the optical tomogram, such as term migration observed in ridge regression for state reconstruction, also appear when using maximum likelihood methods. These outcomes can be classified as classical for the given light state, eliminating the need for further optimization or data points to predict the resulting optical tomogram, which is found to be directly related to the wigner function in such cases.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb experiment. Following particle tagging and flavor identification, scientists analyzed the charge of the $D$ meson to distinguish between $B^0_s$ and its antiparticle, $\bar{B}^0_s$, candidates. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S)/\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \pi^0)$ and $\mathcal{B}(\bar{B}^0_s\to D^0 K^0_S)/\mathcal{B}(\bar{B}^0_s\to D^0 \pi^0)$, given the previously established $B(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \pi^0)$ branching fraction of $5.1\times10^{-4}$. The resulting ratios are found

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices from their join irreducibles, determining all join irreducible submodules of a given module is not a straightforward task. However, for modules that have no module composition multiplicities, we present an alternative approach based on the composition factors, drawing on the information about submodules and their lattices. Given input submodules that encompass all factors and are readily lattice-structure known, the approach allows for the construction of the lattice of submodules of the given module, with its join irreducibles identified. An illustrative example of applying this approach to a given module is provided.
We explore how several established recurrent curvature concepts, including recurrent shape, second fundamental, and ambient tensors, can lead to biharmonic hypersuraches within Euclidean space.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subset of numbers in base p/q that translate to nonnegative integers and demonstrates its language-theoretic status. Building on this foundation, our second main result outlines a method to determine if a given number basep/q does or does not contain a specific rational number. We also explore the application of this approach to relation recognition and discuss its connection to existing research.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 17 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHC's Atlas detector, researchers investigated the production of the $D_s^{*-}$ meson's higher-order weak decay into the $K^{-}\pi^{+}\pi\pi^{+}$ final state. The $D_s^{*-}$ meson primarily decays into the $K^{-}\pi^{+}$ state via weak weak decay and subsequently into the $K^{-}\pi^{+}\pi\pi^{+}$ final state via weak weak decay. By analyzing the $K^{-}\pi^{+}\pi\pi^{+}$ final state, physicists were able to study the $D_s^{*-}$ meson and its charge conjugate. A new measurement of the $s\bar{c}}$ quark-antiquark bound state's production cross section was performed in proton-proton collisions, building upon the $s_c}$ state produced in the same environment. A branching fraction of the $D_s^{*-}$ meson's decay into the $K^{-}\pi^{+}\pi\pi^{+}$ final state was measured with a value of $(4.93 \pm 0.29 \pm 0.15 \pm 0.26 \pm 0.12)\%$, accounting for various sources of uncertainty.
