A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under constant force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the dynamics are chaotic in nature, characterized by a confirmed presence of correlation dimension and rate of Lyapunov. These discoveries hold significant potential for applying acoustic signals from material failure processes to quality control and safety protocols in industrial settings, particularly for materials exhibiting brittle fracture behavior.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems related to the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. The first problem was resolved by Menger himself in 1931, but the second problem remained unsolved until 1957, when J. A. Rogers provided the solution. As a consequence of this finding, a novel and informative function was defined, named the "deficit," which serves a purpose similar to that of the excess function.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within 30 degrees) from 24.0% to 85.0%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing reliable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be easily implemented and used, with a real-time monitoring system in place to guide testing efforts and ensure their effectiveness. The system's efficiency is greatly enhanced by its geometric shape, which is easily configurable and adaptable to various testing scenarios. The theory's practical application has been demonstrated through a compiler toolchain that is easily accessible and usable, with an existing proof assistant that is widely used in the community. The system's efficiency and reliability make it an invaluable asset for developing safe programming languages that are widely used in various industries, including finance, healthcare, and transportation. The theory's success also paves the way for future research into even safer programming languages that are highly adaptable and versatile, with wide-ranging applications in critical systems and infrastructure.

We address a technical issue raised by Serre's conjecture as reinterpreted by Diamond and Pollack, which kummer theory helped resolve. A direct kummer theory connection to the polynomial behavior of local zeta factors in L-function theory suggests a potential path forward in addressing Serre's conjecture as it applies to higher dimensional GL_n spaces.

Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental. Building on our previous work, our new imaging technique develops a fast self-sensing method to distinguish between different types of damage such as delamination and cracks in fiber-reinforced composites. 
By applying conductive nanofillers that experience asymmetric electrical resistance changes in relation to damage type, EIT images can accurately distinguish between different types of delamination and delaminations combined with cracks. 
The capacity to differentiate damage types enhances the functionality of self-sensing materials and contributes to more effective health monitoring systems capable of determining an composite's state in engineering projects.

This work proposes a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces centered on geometric vector techniques and illustrates the method's efficacy through a variety of vector integrand identities proven using this framework.

If a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree that is not a line has a non-trivial action, we prove that its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree.

The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm, named 'SN-NS', based on the Neumann Series, which employs non-uniform step sizes to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis and multiple convergence proofs have been established for 'SN-NS', demonstrating its superiority over other methods in terms of speed and efficiency. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets have validated the effectiveness of 'SN-NS'.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen significant development especially in large data settings. This paper advances the understanding of settings where context learning occurs in distributed environments with context spaces too vast for exact memory. Here context encoding is approximated with binary codes. Using approximately 5d bits per context and exact context knowledge among distributed nodes, this research provides performance bounds. These improvements surpass existing research by a factor of at least 10^4. An online learning algorithm is proposed with these optimized performance bounds. This learning algorithm is designed for situations where context spaces are too large for exact knowledge even among distributed nodes. This research fills a crucial gap in research regarding context linear bandits in such settings.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems and may contribute to the process of dust particles growing larger. However, it's found that once dust particles reach a certain size around 1 mm, the VSI has less of an effect on particle mixing. This is because less gas motion reduces the potential for dust to redistribute itself. To address this issue, a comprehensive model has been created that takes into account dust particle growth and VSI-driven mixing to analyze the evolution of particles and their settling over time. When located in regions where dust growth is slow, the VSI helps accelerate the process of settling. This leads to brighter surfaces in those areas and may cause rapid migration of particles to faster-settling zones. This process can result in a cycle of settling, pile-up, and possible expulsion or planet formation within a short period of time. In fast-cycling areas, the cycle can lead to the formation of planets within less than a million years, while in slow-cycling areas, the cycle can cause the process of settling to continue over longer periods of time. Region profiles have been obtained to illustrate the varying characteristics of dust growth, cycling speed, and particle size in different areas of the protoplanetary disk system.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service have created innovative threats such as hidden functionalities that are embedded in artificial neural networks. In typical research scenarios, triggers for these embedded features are often visible and easily identifiable, leading to a situation where more sophisticated characteristics are in demand. In a research project called Neural Race, competitors strive to develop backdoor activations that are undetectable, which are fully functional yet impossible to identify in the neural network. This objective results in a detrimental effect where each component of the backdoor mechanism needs to be fully optimized to prevent any standing out and becoming easily discoverable. In a race-like environment, neural networks that are affected by backdoor activations are in a constant state of evolution, making it hard for them to remain effective if not continuously supported. This neural race between the affected networks and the researchers who deploy the backdoor activations aims to find an optimum configuration that is fully functional but also undetectable in the learning environment.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server, compounded by the fact that not all nodes possess sufficient data or power to participate consistently. A study was conducted using a shuffling approach where a subset of nodes periodically sends their local model updates to the server, while the server then broadcasts the updated global model to the nodes. A theoretical framework was developed to guide this process, with several efficient algorithms proposed specifically for linear and logistic regression problems. A proof was also provided demonstrating that these algorithms converge to the optimal solution despite limited communication between nodes and the server. Furthermore, a study was carried out using real-world datasets to validate the effectiveness of these algorithms.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen critique, this non-locality had already been recognized as an instantaneous and dramatic effect when a previously entangled part of a particle's wave function collapsed following the measurement or alteration of the remaining part, as per the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics and the concept of wave function collapse. In an effort to further elucidate the startling nature of this non-locality, Einstein utilized a modified version of his 'spooky action' experiment proposed by Bell in 1964, designed to demonstrate the instantaneous non-local collapse of wave functions and its potential violation of the speed of light limit inherent in special relativity, which would have suggested the existence of quantum effects that are inherently non-local and instantaneous. However, such effects that are inherently non-local and instantaneous are deemed impossible according to the principles of special relativity. Since the quantum world has been confirmed to adhere to the rules outlined by special relativity, it can be concluded that our current understanding or utilization of non-local wave function collapse effects is likely flawed or inaccurate, as per the argument put forth by Einstein in 1927. In line with this line of reasoning

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded significant benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy-preserving algorithms like Federated Learning (FL), which can optimize traffic management, vehicle routing, and driver assistance systems without compromising sensitive IoVs data. However, as IoVs data plays a pivotal role in machine learning models, excluding it from training processes may result in biased outcomes and compromised performance, particularly in scenarios involving unrepresented groups. In an effort to address this challenge, the Internet of Vehicles Federated Learning context presents a novel threat model called a Thorny Client Threat, which encompasses both curtailment and total deprivation of training opportunities for specific IoVs devices. Upon identifying several practical attacks feasible on FL systems, researchers have also proposed an innovative countermeasure scheme guaranteeing equitable FL opportunities for all participating IoVs devices with theoretical proofs of security and fairness, along with evaluations demonstrating the effectiveness of this countermeasure in ensuring equitable FL performance.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests.

R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly focusing, we establish that solutions in a bounded subset of the obstacle's exterior will also experience finite-time blowup given the same initial conditions.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors are valued for their capacity to provide unambiguous evidence in support of competing assumptions. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is not straightforward, as it requires a prior cognitive science analysis that may be difficult to specify and validate. This uncertainty about the prior can hinder the use of Bayes factors for decision-making. This talk proposes a framework that integrates Bayes factor analysis and probabilistic point estimates of cognitive science parameters to overcome this uncertainty. This approach remains applicable even when priors are in question, while also simplifying the justification for Bayes factor results. A case study using this framework will be presented, along with examples of its application in cognitive science research.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection according to the five-point taxonomy by Carmichael (1970). This process results in a dataset comprising 6000+ sentences pairs with appropriate discourse indicators that predate the inception of the CoNNL 2012 task. This collection can be used to train a CNN-based classifier that achieves accurate predictions of discourse indicators between sentences that have a recognized semantic relationship. Through this process, concepts such as "by contrast" and "in part" can be classified with an accuracy of 93.6% and 84.6% respectively, demonstrating the importance of understanding semantic relations for effective discourse analysis. This research paves the way for automatic generation of discourse annotations and suggests that semantic information and discourse indicators complement rather than compete with each other.

Building upon the Jordanian twist concept introduced in literature, we have derived a generalized version. The generalized version, dependent on two parameters, is presented as a specific case of a generalization resulting from a two-parameter diagonal twist of an $L$-brace structure of an algebraic algebra. The two-parameter generalized version meets the two-cocycle condition and yields an equivalent twisted algebra with reduced dimension compared to the original algebra.

This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets, utilizing graph theory and model checking to analyze and visualize language relationships. Given two enhanced regular expressions representing a and b, the algorithm determines if a's language is included within b's language, leveraging Brzozowski's derivative concept and generating regular expression graphs for analysis. Utilizing algorithms from model checking, a second-pass process computes language representations, allowing for an effective decision process regarding language containment. Empirical testing over generated datasets demonstrates the efficacy of this approach in comparing and contrasting with conventional methods.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we develop a comprehensive integral representation of conformal block operators in CFT$_2$, specifically tailored for spinning primary fields. Notably, this integral expression can be re-expressed as a product of two weighted AdS$_2$ field combinations when the primary fields in question are conserved, which results in the representation of conserved current conformal block operators in CFT$_2$ in terms of geodesic operators defined within the AdS$_2$ framework rather than the AdS$_3$ framework. Moreover, this new perspective enables a direct link between AdS$_2$ geodesic operators and polynomials of Ads$_2$ geodesic kick operators proposed in the context of the HKLL bulk field reconstruction scheme. Consequently, this allows us to derive a fully explicit integral expression of the AdS$_3$, specifically for the W$_2$ conformal block, in terms of polynomials that involve AdS$_2$ geodesic kick operators.

To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors utilizing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections, each with a slightly different geometry, to direct X-rays toward various image sensors. Using LE's inherent focusing properties and the varying shapes of the sections, we can reduce cross-talk and enable efficient wide-field X-ray monitoring. A theoretical study shows that a 10-degree radius wide-field X-ray monitor with a 0.1 degree field of view could be built without a degraded time resolution compared to current systems. This system would do so with just 12 MuLE modules and 9600 mirrors, significantly fewer than the 60000 mirrors needed for a single LE optic. Furthermore, we can expand the system's coverage by adding more sections to each LE mirror without increasing the number of image sensors required.

To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework was implemented and used to explore the impact of velocity and density information on the formation of halos through $N$-body cosmological simulations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time during the simulations. The study focused on dark matter halos in $\Lambda$CDM simulations and used $2048^3$ grids to conduct multiple independent simulations. The simulations varied the halo mass prediction and the power spectrum of the initial conditions, with one experiment incorporating velocity information and another excluding it. The study found that using models that included velocity information resulted in more accurate halo mass predictions, particularly for lower mass halos, and that the inclusion of velocity fields had a significant impact on the halo mass function. The research also found that the differences between models with and without velocity information were consistent across simulations with different initial condition powers, leading to the development of an improved halo-mass predictor called $MNP$ that incorporates only density fields while still producing halo mass functions that closely match those obtained from full $N$-body simulations.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that expels atoms from the trap, resulting in a loss that occurs in the microsecond to millisecond timescale. A novel method has been developed to measure this loss to precisely determine the expelled magnetic field. This loss-based magnetometry technique achieved a recording depth of 200 nm and a measurement time of 100 microseconds, enabling the detection of expelled fields as weak as 10-100 uG within this timescale. This approach offers advantages over conventional methods by eliminating the need for slow imaging processes and allowing for the monitoring of dynamic changes in material properties through real-time observation.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer, satisfactory agreement with experimental results regarding YSR state splitting was found. However, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, spin-orbit coupling was insufficient to account for observed state splitting. Reversal of the magnetic dimer's moment alignment led to YSR state splitting, along with a notable shift in energy and formation of a zero-energy bound state. This bound state emerged due to the $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state crossing the Fermi level and becoming the lowest energy state.

This report details our approach and outcomes for our entry into task 1 of the 2019 ISIC challenge, aimed at assisting in skin cancer diagnosis through image analysis. We explored various deep learning architectures, including convolutional neural networks (CNN), and experimented with different training strategies, such as self-training and ensemble training. Our final outputs were formed by combining the predictions of multiple trained models. We submitted multiple outcomes for each input image to capture the probabilistic nature of diagnosis results. Our collective findings demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in providing accurate and reliable predictions for skin cancer diagnosis. Code, models, and a discussion of our approach are available for download at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3331206.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-10 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering and radiation at both leading and next-to-leading order levels, as well as through direct vector boson decay processes.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant manifolds such as the origin, straight lines, parabolas, and hyperbolas in systems with fractional orders between 0 and 1.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequalities derived from control theory. An operator theoretic approach is employed to derive the required observability inequalities.

According to the simplest version of the scoto-seesaw model, two neutrino mass scales and one new particle scale are introduced. The lowest of these two neutrino oscillation lengths corresponds to the atmospheric mass scale, while the higher one is linked to the solar mass scale. To verify this two-scale scoto-seesaw model, we need to examine the role of the new particle scale. Our analysis shows that within the range of the new particle scale, the scoto-seesaw model is inconsistent with both the solar neutrino data and the neutrinoless double beta decay data, with one possible exception. However, we can resolve this issue by slightly adjusting the parameters or by adding a new particle. The option of expanding the model by introducing an extra neutral scalar field that interacts in a way that breaks the symmetry is particularly effective in doing so.
